doc.title: Denny Zeitlin interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Parents refuse to groom him as a classical pianist
summary: His teacher urged six or seven hours of practice daily, parents declined, and he explains he never wanted to reinterpret the written page.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Yeah it could have. It could have been terrible for me. And there was another juncture where they again made the right decision. After a few years of studying classical music my teacher took my parents aside and said well now is the time you have to begin to groom your son for his classical musical career. He should be practicing six, seven hours a day. He shouldn’t be playing baseball after school, he should be coming home and studying this instrument. And my folks looked at each other and thought about me and said enh enh, that’s not for him, that’s not where his heart lies. And they were absolutely right. I mean I have great respect and admiration for musicians who have the gene for the reinterpretation of the written page. I don’t have it. When I studied classical music, as soon as I would learn a piece, all I wanted to do was to take that material structurally and harmonically and rhythmically and use it in my own music. The idea of keeping a formal repertoire up and ready to perform left me cold. I just had no interest in that.
No kidding. By the age of — at what age did you kind of realize it, or was it always that way for you?
It was always that way. I would learn the music but then I would be using it in compositions and other kinds of stuff and improvising off of these.
So if you were playing a piece of Bach, were you at the point where you could look horizontally down the music and recognize the chord structures and those kinds of things?
